summary:
We built Red Outpost, a browser game where children aged 7 to 12 run a small base on Mars or the Moon. Players walk around the outpost, make oxygen, grow food, store power and protect the crew from radiation. Turning up one system leaves less power for the others, so keeping everyone safe takes planning.

Missions replay solar events from NASA's DONKI archive. Real terrain maps shape the ground, and research cards connect the player's choices to NASA experiments and Canadian Space Agency resources. Earth replies take time, supplies can arrive incomplete, and the debrief explains what happened.

Teachers can give a class the same mission and compare printable results. We wanted children to experience why space missions need careful decisions, then follow their questions back to the real science. The game runs in a browser without an account or special equipment.
details:
Red Outpost puts the player in charge of a small crew for 12 game days. They can choose Gale Crater or Jezero Crater on Mars, or a base near the lunar south pole. The astronaut walks between working stations inside the habitat and goes outside to clean solar panels, repair equipment and collect samples. A normal game day lasts about 90 seconds, so changes to the base have consequences the player can see during a session.

The base shares one power supply. Oxygen production, greenhouse lighting, water cleaning and radiation protection all draw from it. Solar panels charge the battery during daylight; dust and darkness reduce the available power. Turning up the shield during a storm can leave less energy for growing food. Going outside to clean the panels helps the base but uses oxygen and exposes the astronaut to radiation. Lettuce grows quickly, while potatoes provide more food but recover more slowly after poor conditions.

Communication adds another decision. Large or unsafe dial changes need approval from Earth, and the game continues while a reply travels back. For Mars, the delay is estimated from NASA JPL orbital data for the mission date. The Moon uses a much shorter light travel time. Players can override a request, but it costs crew trust and science points. Supply requests also take time and can deliver less than expected; these shipments are simulated locally.

Real observations are part of the mission. Eight selected DONKI months are bundled with the game, and players can fetch other historical months. The game selects a few strong recorded events and maps them into a playable schedule. It preserves their source dates and labels the historical month. These are observations from spacecraft near Earth, replayed in a fictional mission. Storm strength, compressed time, the powered shield and mission radiation limit are teaching rules, not predictions of conditions at a real base.

The terrain uses reduced elevation grids for Gale, Jezero and the Shackleton rim, with a flat area blended in for the base. At the end, a debrief explains resource use and the cause of failure or success. It also links to NASA research on plants, muscles and radiation, and to Canadian Space Agency work on food production and lunar exploration. Children can try the same weather again and see whether a different plan works.

Classroom mode lets a teacher fix the site, difficulty, historical month and random seed. Everyone starts with standard equipment, making results easier to compare. Teachers can turn explanations on or off and print a mission summary. We designed the controls for keyboard and touch, added reduced-motion support and kept the 3D scene simple to limit the load on school devices. The intended benefit is practical discussion about limited resources and cause and effect; learning outcomes have not yet been measured in a completed classroom study.

We used TypeScript, HTML and CSS, with Three.js for the 3D world and Vite for the build. The simulation is separate from the renderer and is checked with Vitest. JavaScript and Python scripts prepare science data, terrain, original art, sound and presentation files. Progress and settings are saved in the browser. The project is hosted on Netlify, and the team used Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to help develop and review the code.
